intro: This is the complete first side of Rachmaninoff’s 1919 Edison recording, not the whole rhapsody. The original source identifies Edison Diamond Disc 82169-R; later music lies on other sides.
question: How does Rachmaninoff distribute weight and space within the opening disc side?

cues.title: One Edison side only
cues.text: The source identifies Rachmaninoff, Edison Diamond Disc 82169-R and “part I”. This player preserves that side as one stream; it does not splice together the remainder of the rhapsody.
cues.evidence: Commons transcribes the Library of Congress source identification and dates the recording 1919. This is a carrier boundary, not a claim that Liszt’s work ends here.

cues.title: Weight near the opening
cues.text: The early passage contains the largest measured crest on this side. Follow the spaces between its gestures as well as their weight; this transfer’s surface noise is not part of Liszt’s piano writing.
cues.evidence: The report’s highest relative-level windows are 0:45–1:00, with a maximum at 0:50. This identifies the recorded contour, not acoustic piano dynamics.

cues.title: A marked withdrawal
cues.text: The side turns to a quieter continuation after the early crest. Compare the length of this lighter stretch with the more forceful phrases around it.
cues.evidence: A 1:02 novelty boundary precedes a drop from −14.2 dB at 1:00 to −28.2 at 1:05; the following passage stays relatively low.

cues.title: The sound gathers again
cues.text: The recorded weight rises again across this stretch. Listen for how a renewed phrase grows from quieter activity, without assuming that stronger sound means faster playing.
cues.evidence: The report’s largest novelty boundary is 2:18. Relative level rises from −25.6 dB at 2:10 to −16.6 at 2:25 while detected attacks do not rise correspondingly.

cues.title: A side is not a movement
cues.text: Keep the comparison confined to the shared opening passage. The later part of this stream approaches a disc-side ending, not the rhapsody’s final conclusion; whole-file durations would compare unequal stretches of music.
cues.evidence: The source identifies part I only. The 249.4-second report measures this one side; no full-work duration or final cadence is claimed.

composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.
composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
